rows.selection_reason: With no prior evidence, the most important first step is to establish a clear performance floor. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest possible configuration: a linear-dimensionality-reduced RNA representation with no learned encoder, no aggregation, and no fusion. This gives a well-defined baseline that (1) tells me whether RNA signal alone is informative for the task, (2) provides a reference accuracy against which all more complex choices (learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, fusion) can be measured, and (3) is the fastest and least risky experiment to run, preserving budget for later exploration. In experiment 2 I can then swap in a learned RNA encoder (e.g., scvi_n200 or scgpt) while holding everything else constant, cleanly isolating the effect of representation quality.

We have only one data point (config_001: RNA-only, PCA, single profile → 48.5% acc), so the largest uncertainty is whether the image modality carries comparable or superior signal. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean modality comparison: it matches config_001 in profile setting and model simplicity while isolating the effect of switching from RNA to image representation. If image-only substantially outperforms 48.5%, it justifies investing remaining budget in multimodal fusion and stronger image encoders. If it underperforms, it confirms RNA as the dominant signal and redirects effort toward better RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt) and multiprofile aggregation. This single experiment resolves the most critical branching decision in the search space with minimal confounding variables.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, single) achieves 48.5% acc while image (resnet50, single) is very weak at 20.8% acc. The critical uncertainty is whether the image modality is fundamentally uninformative for this task or whether ResNet50 is simply an inadequate encoder. Testing config_013 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) isolates the image encoder variable while keeping profile setting constant, directly answering whether a stronger pretrained encoder (ViT-L) can make the image modality viable. This is the highest-impact decision for the remaining 7 experiments: if ViT-L also performs poorly, I can confidently abandon image/multimodal paths and focus all remaining budget on RNA encoder and profile improvements; if ViT-L performs well, multimodal fusion becomes a promising high-ceiling direction. This single experiment resolves a binary strategic fork that would otherwise waste budget.

Evidence: RNA-only with PCA (config_001, acc=0.485) dominates both image-only baselines (acc≈0.21-0.23), establishing RNA as the primary signal. The RNA encoder choice is the most fundamental untested design variable. Question: Does a learned nonlinear encoder (scvi_n200) capture structure that linear PCA misses, improving on the 0.485 baseline? This is a clean single-variable comparison to config_001 (only the encoder changes, keeping singleprofile and no aggregation). Why this is the best next step: With 6 experiments remaining, identifying the superior RNA encoder before exploring multiprofile or multimodal fusion ensures we build subsequent experiments on the strongest foundation. If scvi_n200 outperforms PCA, it opens a promising branch (configs 005-006, 028-039); if not, we confirm PCA suffices and can redirect budget toward profile aggregation or fusion. Testing image-based multimodal fusion is deprioritized given the large performance gap.

Evidence: scvi_n200 is the best RNA encoder so far (0.5203 acc vs 0.4849 for pca_n2000), and image-only models are weak (~0.21-0.23), confirming RNA as the dominant signal. Uncertainty: we have not yet tested whether multiprofile aggregation adds value over the single-profile baseline for the best encoder. This experiment (config_005: rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a minimal, clean extension of config_004—changing only the profile setting from single to multi with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). It isolates the effect of multiprofile without confounding with a complex transformer aggregator. If avgpool helps, it justifies testing transformer next (config_006); if it doesn't, we save budget for exploring multimodal fusion or scgpt. With 5 experiments remaining, this is the highest-information, lowest-risk next step to determine whether profile aggregation is a productive axis of improvement.

Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved the best accuracy so far at 0.6501, a large jump over its singleprofile counterpart config_004 (0.5203), confirming that multiprofile aggregation with scvi_n200 is the most promising direction. Image-only models are far weaker (≤0.23), so the immediate priority is optimizing the RNA pipeline before committing budget to multimodal fusion. Question: config_006 tests whether transformer aggregation outperforms avgpool for the same scvi_n200 multiprofile setup, isolating the aggregation method as the only variable. Why this experiment: it is a clean A/B comparison against config_005, resolving a critical design choice that will directly inform which aggregation to pair with any future multimodal or scgpt experiments. With 4 experiments remaining, locking in the best aggregation strategy now maximizes the value of subsequent multimodal or encoder-swap experiments.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_006 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) at 0.653 acc. Multiprofile with scvi_n200 gave a large jump over singleprofile (~13 pts), aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) is essentially a wash, and image-only models are very weak (≤0.227). The one untested RNA encoder is scgpt, and we have no data on whether it could outperform scvi_n200. Question: Does scgpt, in the same multiprofile+transformer setting as config_006, beat or match scvi_n200? This is a clean single-variable comparison (only the RNA encoder changes), directly isolating encoder quality in the best-performing configuration. Why this is the best use of experiment 7: With only 3 experiments left, confirming or ruling out a better encoder before committing remaining budget to multimodal fusion or other extensions is the highest-information step. If scgpt wins, we pivot remaining experiments around it; if it loses, we lock in scvi_n200 and can spend the last 2-3 experiments testing whether multimodal fusion with the best RNA setup adds any value.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_006 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) at 0.653 accuracy, with multiprofile providing the largest single boost (+0.13 over singleprofile) and scvi_n200 clearly superior to both pca_n2000 and scgpt. Image-only models are very weak (~0.21-0.23), raising the question of whether adding image information to the strong RNA signal helps or merely adds noise. This experiment (config_039) tests the most promising multimodal extension: it pairs the best RNA encoder (scvi_n200) with multiprofile + transformer aggregation (the top RNA-only recipe) and the best image encoder (imagenet_vit_l, marginally better than resnet50), using weighted fusion to allow the model to down-weight the weak image channel. This is the best use of experiment 8 because it directly tests whether multimodal fusion can exceed the 0.653 RNA-only ceiling. If it succeeds, the remaining 2 experiments can refine fusion/aggregation; if it fails, we confirm RNA-only is optimal and can spend the last 2 experiments on minor RNA-only tweaks (e.g., config_003 to confirm scvi > pca in multiprofile, or re-testing with different hyperparameters).

The current best is config_039 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.7250 accuracy. The single most impactful untested variation on this top configuration is the fusion method: config_038 is identical except it uses concat instead of weighted fusion. RNA-only experiments showed aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) matters little (~0.3% difference), but fusion strategy in multimodal settings is a more fundamental design axis that we have only tested in one form (weighted). Testing concat isolates whether learned weighted fusion is genuinely superior or whether a simpler concatenation could match or exceed it. This is the best use of experiment 9 because it directly challenges the current best with a single-variable change, and the result will inform the final experiment: if concat wins, we've found a new best; if weighted holds, we can use the last experiment to probe other dimensions (e.g., avgpool vs transformer in the multimodal setting via config_037).

The current best is config_039 (multimodal, multiprofile, SCVI_n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.7250 accuracy. The strongest evidence shows SCVI_n200 is the best RNA encoder, ViT-L is the best image encoder, multiprofile + transformer aggregation is optimal for RNA, and weighted fusion marginally beats concat. The only untested variant keeping all best components is config_037, which swaps transformer for avgpool aggregation while retaining SCVI_n200, ViT-L, multiprofile, and weighted fusion. In RNA-only, transformer edged out avgpool (0.6530 vs 0.6501), but the multimodal setting may interact differently with the image stream. As the final experiment, this isolates the aggregation choice in the full multimodal pipeline—either confirming transformer's importance or revealing that avgpool is competitive—making it the highest-value exploitation test with the best chance of matching or exceeding the current best.
